newsitem.title: KENYA: FEATURE - Rebels alleged to have killed Zaire refugees.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Rebels alleged to have killed Zaire refugees.

text.p: Aid workers, human rights and U.N. officials say they are convinced that rebels slaughtered thousands of Hutu refugees in the former Zaire before seizing power in May.

Some aid workers, and residents, refugees and witnesses also said Rwandan Tutsi troops fighting for the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL) took part in and directed some killings of Rwandan refugees.
"There is a consistent pattern of killing refugees...It is difficult to say how many, but certainly thousands and probably tens of thousands," said an expatriate human rights worker.
Added a field worker in Zaire during the war: "It is an absolute certainty that Rwandan soldiers were fighting in eastern Zaire and there is absolutely no doubt that they killed refugees."
Other aid workers confirm the massacres, but dispute charges of Rwandan involvement. All 19 foreign workers interviewed asked for anonymity to avoid compromising their agencies' operations.
Reports of the massacres, denied by the rebels and Rwandan officials, circulated for months as rebels swept westward in a seven-month advance that ended Mobutu Sese Seko's 32-year reign.

The United Nations is soon expected to investigate the reports on the ground following negotiations with the government of AFDL leader Laurent Kabila, president of what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

But in a report based on interviews in May with survivors in Rwanda and U.N. staff, U.N. human rights investigator Roberto Garreton of Chile said he had received information on 134 incidents of massacres of Rwandan refugees by AFDL forces.

The report this month said evidence appeared to point to genocide and systematic executions of refugees. Kabila's government dismissed the report as untrue and accused Garreton, who was barred by Kinshasa, of trying to tarnish its image.
KAGAME SAYS U.N. DEFLECTING BLAME
Rwandan Vice President and Defence Minister Paul Kagame last week acknowledged Rwanda had played a central role in the war and said Rwandan troops helped capture at least four cities.

Kagame did not deny individual atrocities were possible. But he told the Washington Post that Rwanda had warned the United Nations and Western countries to demilitarise eastern Zaire refugee camps and separate Hutu fighters from civilians.

"It is my strong belief that the United Nations people are trying to deflect the blame for failures of their own making onto us," said Kagame, who led Tutsi rebels who seized power in Rwanda in 1994 and ended a three-month genocide by Hutus.

While about 600,000 of the original 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees returned home from eastern Zaire last November, an estimated 500,000 fled west including extremist Hutu Interahamwe militiamen and former Rwandan Hutu troops responsible for the genocide, according to the U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR).

Aid workers said AFDL troops pursued Rwandan Hutu refugees for more than 1,200 km (750 miles) and at intervals massacred them because of their ethnic connection with the genocide, in which an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus died.

Allegations of the killings were supported by testimony from dozens of witnesses and numerous other interviews with Reuters in the former Zaire between last October, when the AFDL launched its rebellion, and May 17 when the rebels seized Kinshasa.
Reuters was also shown what aid workers and villagers said were mass graves where they had buried Rwandan refugees who had been killed.
The country's foreign minister, Bizima Karaha, told Reuters the only mass graves on its soil were for cholera victims or those killed by Hutu extremists who held refugees hostage.
INCIDENTS ALLEGED AT FIVE SITES

Nevertheless incidents in at least five parts of the country between last November and May led aid officials to conclude even before a U.N. investigation that thousands of Rwandan refugees were killed.

CHIMANGA CAMP - AFDL troops using a mortar or grenades and automatic rifles are alleged to have killed more than 300 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees at Chimanga Camp, 40 km (25 miles) southwest of Bukavu last November, according to aid agencies, a survivor and local villagers who showed Reuters a series of mass graves they said they had dug.

KISANGANI - Alliance troops massacred hundreds of refugees from Kasese and Biaro camps south of Kisangani in the northeast in late April and drove some 80,000 away, though thousands were too sick to walk, aid workers, survivors and villagers said.
Witnesses have reported seeing what looked like mass graves south of Biaro and said rebels burned corpses of refugees who had been killed.
UNHCR repatriated 45,000 refugees by air from Kisangani but 44,000 refugees remain unaccounted for.
Kabila has repeatedly denied refugees were killed south of Kisangani, and senior AFDL officials said rebel forces were themselves attacked by former Rwandan troops and militiamen.
MASISI - One aid official described the Masisi region west of the eastern town of Goma as the "epicentre of the killings" of refugees with thousands of Rwandan and Zairean Hutus killed.
Another foreign worker with years of experience in the area said in April that AFDL and Rwandan troops committed a series of massacres against local Hutus and Rwandan Hutu refugees there.
Human rights groups and aid workers have reported seeing mass graves in the Masisi, and Zairean witnesses have given detailed testimony of massacres of Rwandan and Zairean Hutus.
"We consider every Hutu (in Masisi) to be a legitimate target," an AFDL commander had told Reuters in April.
SHABUNDA - An aid agency report said agencies were being used to lure refugees hiding in the Shabunda forests west of Bukavu on to roads where they could be killed by AFDL soldiers.
The report, which gave no numbers of those killed, followed an aid trip to Shabunda in which aid workers talked to villagers and AFDL soldiers and saw what were apparently mass graves.
"There was a systematic policy of killing refugees in Shabunda and they killed lots of them," said an aid worker.
One Alliance colonel, who spoke English and said he was Rwandan, told aid workers it was AFDL policy to use aid to attract refugees out of the forest where they could be killed.

MBANDAKA - Witnesses including priests, teachers and civil servants told Reuters "Rwandan" troops slaughtered more than 200 at a port in the northwestern town of Mbandaka on May 13 when they seized the town.
Armed Hutus among the refugees fled before rebels arrived, witnesses said.

Local aid workers at nearby Wendji village showed Reuters graves they said contained 140 bodies of Hutus killed by Alliance troops earlier on May 13 and gave details of the numbers of men, women and children they said they had buried.
One aid agency with wide contacts among the local population said the number killed near Mbandaka ran into thousands.
DIFFERING THEORIES
Aid workers disagreed over whether the alleged massacres were AFDL policy.
In some cases, they said, local alliance leaders appeared to order killings independently of AFDL command, while in others local commanders acted with apparent tacit support of seniors.
In still other cases, some said, it appeared refugee killings were ordered by senior AFDL leaders or Kigali.

A U.N. official said non-Rwandan AFDL troops, wedded militarily to their Rwandan backers, were forced to accept a Rwandan military solution to the refugee problem in return for support in ousting Mobutu.
